title: IV. The Third Son, Alyosha
section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: He was only twenty; his brother Ivan was in his twenty-fourth year at the time, while their elder brother Dmitri was twenty-seven. First, I should explain that this young man, Alyosha, was no fanatic, and, in my opinion at least, wasn't even a mystic. I might as well give my full opinion right from the start. He was simply an early lover of humanity, and the reason he took up monastic life was simply that, at the time, it struck him as the ideal escape for a soul struggling out of the darkness of worldly wickedness into the light of love. And the reason this life struck him that way was that he found in it, as he thought, an extraordinary being: our celebrated elder, Zossima, to whom he attached himself with all the warm first love of his ardent heart. But I don't dispute that he was very strange even then, and had been from the cradle. I've already mentioned, by the way, that though he lost his mother in his fourth year, he remembered her all his life—her face, her caresses—“as though she stood alive before me.” Such memories can persist, as everyone knows, from an even earlier age, from as young as two, but they scarcely stand out across a whole lifetime like isolated points of light in the darkness, like a corner torn out of some vast picture that has otherwise faded and vanished, save for that one fragment. That's how it was with him. He remembered one still summer evening: an open window, the slanting rays of the setting sun—that he recalled most vividly of all—in a corner of the room the holy icon, a lamp burning before it, and, kneeling before the icon, his mother, sobbing hysterically, crying out and moaning, snatching him up in both arms and squeezing him so tightly it hurt, praying for him to the Mother of God, holding him out with both arms toward the icon as if to place him under the Mother's protection… and then suddenly a nurse rushing in and snatching him away from her in fright. That was the picture. And Alyosha remembered his mother's face at that moment. He used to say it was frenzied, but beautiful, as he remembered it. But he rarely cared to speak of this memory to anyone. As a child and a young man he wasn't at all expansive, and talked very little, but not out of shyness or sullen unsociability—quite the opposite—it came from something else, a kind of inner preoccupation, entirely personal and unconcerned with other people, but so important to him that he seemed, in a sense, to forget about them because of it. But he was fond of people; he seemed, his whole life, to place implicit trust in them, and yet no one ever took him for a simpleton or a naive fool. There was something about him that made you feel at once—and it stayed true all his life afterward—that he had no wish to judge others, that he would never take it upon himself to criticize or condemn anyone for anything. He seemed, in fact, to accept everything without the slightest condemnation, though often grieving bitterly over it, and this was so pronounced that no one could ever shock or unsettle him, even in his earliest youth. Arriving at twenty in his father's house—a veritable sink of filthy debauchery—he, chaste and pure as he was, simply withdrew in silence when the sight became unbearable, but without a trace of contempt or condemnation. His father, who had once been in a dependent position himself and was thus touchy and quick to take offense, met him at first with distrust and sullenness. “He doesn't say much,” he used to remark, “and thinks all the more.” But soon—within a fortnight, in fact—he took to hugging and kissing him constantly, with drunken tears and maudlin sentimentality, and yet he plainly felt a real, deep affection for him, of a kind he'd never before been capable of feeling for anyone.

Everyone, in fact, loved this young man wherever he went, and it had been so since his earliest childhood. When he entered the household of his patron and benefactor, Yefim Petrovitch Polenov, he won the hearts of the whole family, so that they came to regard him quite as their own child. Yet he'd entered the house at such a tender age that he couldn't possibly have acted out of calculation or cunning in winning their affection. So the gift of making himself loved, directly and unconsciously, was simply built into him, into his very nature, so to speak. It was the same at school, though he seemed at first glance to be exactly the sort of child that other children distrust, sometimes mock, even dislike. He was dreamy, for instance, and rather solitary. From his earliest childhood he loved to creep off into a corner with a book, and yet he was a general favorite the whole time he was at school. He was rarely playful or lighthearted, but anyone could see at a glance that this wasn't sullenness. On the contrary, he was bright and good-natured. He never tried to show off in front of the other boys. Perhaps because of this he was never afraid of anyone, and yet the boys understood right away that he wasn't proud of his own fearlessness, that he seemed unaware he was bold and brave at all. He never held a grudge over an insult. It might happen that an hour after being wronged he'd speak to the one who'd wronged him, or answer some question of his, with as trusting and open an expression as if nothing had passed between them. And it wasn't that he seemed to have forgotten the slight, or deliberately forgiven it—he simply didn't regard it as a slight at all, and this utterly won the boys over. He had one trait that made every one of his schoolmates, from the lowest class to the highest, want to tease him—not out of malice, but because it amused them. This trait was a wild, almost fanatical modesty and chastity. He couldn't bear to hear certain words, certain conversations about women. There are “certain” words and conversations that, unfortunately, can never quite be stamped out in schools. Boys pure in mind and heart, practically children still, love to talk among themselves, even out loud, about things, pictures, images that even soldiers would sometimes hesitate to mention. More than that, a good deal that soldiers know nothing of is entirely familiar to quite young children of our educated, upper classes. There's no real moral depravity in it, no genuine corrupt cynicism at its core, but there's the appearance of it, and it's often treated among them as something refined, daring, subtle—worth imitating. Seeing that Alyosha Karamazov stuck his fingers in his ears whenever they started on “that,” they'd sometimes crowd round him, pull his hands away, and shout filth into both his ears, while he struggled, slid to the floor, tried to hide, without ever uttering a word of abuse, enduring the insult in silence. But eventually they left him alone, and stopped taunting him as a “regular girl”—in fact they came to regard it, with something like pity, as a weakness in him. He was always among the top students in his class, but never first.

By the time Yefim Petrovitch died, Alyosha had two more years to finish at the provincial gymnasium. The inconsolable widow went almost immediately after his death on a long trip to Italy with her whole household—which consisted only of women and girls. Alyosha went to live in the home of two distant relatives of Yefim Petrovitch, ladies he'd never even met before. On what terms he lived with them, he didn't know himself. It was very characteristic of him, in fact, that he never worried about at whose expense he was living. In this he was a striking contrast to his elder brother Ivan, who'd struggled through poverty during his first two years at university, supporting himself by his own efforts, and who'd been bitterly aware since childhood that he was living off his benefactor's charity. But this odd trait in Alyosha's character shouldn't, I think, be judged too harshly, because the moment you got to know him even slightly, you'd have seen that Alyosha was one of those youths—almost of the religious-enthusiast type—who, if they suddenly came into a large fortune, wouldn't hesitate to give it all away at the first asking, whether for good works or to some clever con artist. In general he seemed hardly to know the value of money—not literally, of course. When given pocket money, which he never asked for, he was either terribly careless with it, so that it vanished in a moment, or else he'd hold onto it for weeks on end, not knowing what to do with it.
In later years Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, a man very touchy on the subject of money and bourgeois respectability, delivered the following judgment after getting to know Alyosha:

“Here, perhaps, is the one man in the world you could leave alone without a penny in the middle of an unfamiliar city of a million people, and he wouldn't come to any harm—he wouldn't die of cold or hunger, because someone would feed and shelter him at once; and if they didn't, he'd find shelter for himself, and it wouldn't cost him any effort or any humiliation. And sheltering him would be no burden to anyone—quite the opposite, it would probably be seen as a pleasure.”

He didn't finish his studies at the gymnasium. A year before the end of the course, he suddenly announced to the ladies that he was going to see his father about a plan that had occurred to him. They were sorry, and reluctant to let him go. The trip wasn't an expensive one, and the ladies wouldn't let him pawn his watch, a parting gift from his benefactor's family. They provided him generously with money, and even outfitted him with new clothes and linen. But he returned half the money they gave him, saying he intended to travel third class. On arriving in town he gave no answer to his father's first question about why he'd come before finishing his studies, and seemed, so people said, unusually thoughtful. It soon became clear he was looking for his mother's grave. He more or less admitted, at the time, that this was the sole reason for his visit. But that can hardly have been the whole of it. It's more likely that he himself didn't understand, and couldn't explain, what had suddenly stirred in his soul and drawn him irresistibly onto a new, unknown, but inevitable path. Fyodor Pavlovitch couldn't show him where his second wife was buried, since he'd never once visited her grave after throwing earth onto her coffin, and over the years had entirely forgotten where she lay.

Fyodor Pavlovitch, incidentally, hadn't been living in our town for some time before this. Three or four years after his wife's death he'd gone off to the south of Russia and eventually turned up in Odessa, where he spent several years. He made the acquaintance, at first, in his own words, “of a bunch of low Jews, Jewesses, and Jewkins,” and ended up being received by “Jews high and low alike.” It's a fair guess that this is the period when he developed his particular knack for making and hoarding money. He finally returned to our town only three years before Alyosha's arrival. His old acquaintances found him looking terribly aged, though he was by no means an old man yet. He carried himself not exactly with more dignity, but with more brazenness. The former buffoon now showed an insolent tendency to make buffoons out of other people. His depravity with women hadn't simply stayed the same—it had grown even more repulsive. In short order he opened a large number of new taverns across the district. It was clear he had something like a hundred thousand roubles, or not much less. Many people in town and the surrounding district were soon in his debt, and had, of course, put up good security. Lately, too, he'd grown somehow bloated, and seemed more erratic, more uneven, had sunk into a kind of incoherence, would start one thing and carry on with another, as though he were letting himself go entirely. He was drunk more and more often. And if it hadn't been for that same servant, Grigory—who by now had aged a good deal himself, and sometimes looked after him almost like a tutor—Fyodor Pavlovitch might have gotten into serious trouble. Alyosha's arrival seemed to affect even his moral side, as though something long dead in this prematurely old man's soul had stirred back to life.

“Do you know,” he'd often say, looking at Alyosha, “that you're like her, ‘the crazy woman'”—that's what he used to call his dead wife, Alyosha's mother. It was Grigory who pointed the “crazy woman's” grave out to Alyosha. He took him to our town cemetery and showed him, in a remote corner, a cast-iron tombstone—cheap but decently kept—with the name and age of the deceased and the date of her death inscribed on it, and below, a four-line verse of the kind commonly used on old-fashioned middle-class graves. To Alyosha's astonishment, this tombstone turned out to be Grigory's own doing. He'd put it up on the poor “crazy woman's” grave at his own expense, after Fyodor Pavlovitch—whom he'd pestered about the grave repeatedly—had gone off to Odessa, abandoning the grave along with all his memories. Alyosha showed no particular emotion at the sight of his mother's grave. He only listened to Grigory's detailed, solemn account of putting up the stone; he stood there with his head bowed and walked away without a word. It was perhaps a year before he visited the cemetery again. But this small episode wasn't without its effect on Fyodor Pavlovitch—and a rather original effect at that. He suddenly took a thousand roubles to our monastery to pay for requiems for the soul of his wife—not the second one, Alyosha's mother, the “crazy woman,” but the first, Adelaïda Ivanovna, who used to beat him. That same evening he got drunk and cursed out the monks to Alyosha. He himself was far from religious; he'd probably never once put a penny candle in front of a saint's icon. Sudden bursts of feeling and sudden thoughts are common enough in men of that sort.

I've already mentioned that he looked bloated. His face at this time bore unmistakable marks of the life he'd led. Besides the long, fleshy pouches under his small, always insolent, suspicious, ironic eyes, besides the mass of fine wrinkles in his small fat face, his Adam's apple hung below his sharp chin like a great fleshy goiter, giving him a peculiarly repulsive, sensual look; add to that a long, greedy mouth with full lips, between which you could glimpse little stumps of blackened, decayed teeth. He drooled every time he started talking. He liked, in fact, to make fun of his own face, though I believe he was perfectly satisfied with it. He was especially fond of pointing to his nose, which wasn't very large but was quite delicate and conspicuously hooked. “A proper Roman nose,” he used to say, “with my goiter I've got quite the look of an ancient Roman patrician from the age of decline.” He seemed proud of it.

Not long after visiting his mother's grave, Alyosha suddenly announced that he wanted to enter the monastery, and that the monks were prepared to take him in as a novice. He explained that this was his firm wish, and that he was formally asking his father's consent. The old man already knew that the elder Zossima, who lived in the monastery hermitage, had made a special impression on his “gentle boy.”

“That's the most honest monk among them, no question,” he remarked, after listening to Alyosha in thoughtful silence, seeming scarcely surprised by his request. “Hm!… So that's where you want to go, my gentle boy?”

He was half drunk, and suddenly he broke into his slow, half-drunken grin, not without a certain slyness and tipsy cunning in it. “Hm!… I had a feeling you'd end up something like this. Would you believe it? You were making straight for it. Well, no matter, you've got your two thousand roubles. That's a dowry for you. And I'll never desert you, my angel. I'll pay whatever's needed for you there, if they ask for it. But if they don't ask, why should we bother them, eh? What do you say? You know, you spend money like a canary, two grains a week. Hm!… Do you know that near one monastery there's a place, outside the town, where every baby in the place knows there's nothing living there but the 'monks' wives,' as they call them. Thirty women, I believe. I've been there myself. You know, it's interesting in its own way, of course, as a novelty. The worst of it is, it's terribly Russian. No French women there. Of course they could get some easily enough, they've got plenty of money. If word gets to them, they'll come running. Well, there's nothing of that sort here, no 'monks' wives,' and two hundred monks. They're honest men. They keep the fasts, I'll grant them that… Hm… So you want to be a monk? And you know, I'm sorry to lose you, Alyosha; would you believe it, I've really grown fond of you? Well, it's a good opportunity, though. You'll pray for us sinners; we've sinned plenty here. I've always wondered who'd pray for me, whether there's anyone in the world to do it. My dear boy, I'm awfully stupid about that. You wouldn't believe how stupid. You see, however dim-witted I am about it, I keep thinking—I keep thinking, from time to time, of course, not all the while. It's impossible, I think, for the devils to forget to drag me down to hell with their hooks when I die. And then I wonder—hooks? Where would they get them? Made of what? Iron hooks? Do they have some kind of foundry down there? The monks in the monastery probably believe there's a ceiling in hell, for instance. Now, I'm ready to believe in hell, but without a ceiling. It's more refined that way, more enlightened—more Lutheran, so to speak. And really, what does it matter whether it has a ceiling or not? But you know, there's a damnable question tangled up in it. If there's no ceiling, there can be no hooks, and if there are no hooks, the whole thing falls apart—which is unlikely too, since then there'd be no one to drag me down to hell, and if they don't drag me down, where's the justice in the world? _Il faudrait les inventer_, those hooks, purpose-built for me alone, because if you only knew, Alyosha, what a scoundrel I am.”
“But there are no hooks there,” said Alyosha, looking at his father gently and seriously.

“Yes, yes, only the shadows of hooks, I know, I know. That's how a Frenchman once described hell: '_J'ai vu l'ombre d'un cocher qui avec l'ombre d'une brosse frottait l'ombre d'une carrosse._' How do you know there are no hooks, my darling boy? Once you've lived with the monks you'll sing a different tune. But go and find out the truth of it there, and then come and tell me. It's easier, anyway, going into the next world if you know what's waiting for you there. Besides, it'll suit you better with the monks than here with me, with a drunken old man and young harlots—though you're like an angel, nothing touches you. And I dare say nothing will touch you there either. That's why I'm letting you go—because I'm hoping for that. You've got all your wits about you. You'll burn, and you'll burn out; you'll be healed, and come back again. And I'll be waiting for you. I feel that you're the only creature in the world who hasn't condemned me. My dear boy, I feel it, you know. I can't help feeling it.”
And he even started blubbering. He was sentimental. He was wicked, and he was sentimental.
